EXPERT_ID.note: // A complete program. Everything in this language is a rewrite rule: ::= separates what is replaced from what replaces it, and ~ means “print this instead of rewriting”.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Thue (John Colagioia, 2000) is a string-rewriting language: a program is a set of substitution rules ::=, text after ~ is output, and execution rewrites the initial string until no rule applies. It is Turing complete despite having no variables, no numbers and no control flow.

EXPERT_ID.note: // That really is (almost) the whole program. This language is postfix and stack-based: literals push, single symbols operate, and ß flushes the output.
EXPERT_ID.fact: FALSE (Wouter van Oortmerssen, 1993) is a stack-based language of single-character symbols, created to prove how small a compiler could be — the original was about a kilobyte. A string literal pushes its characters, and ß flushes output.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Excerpt of a program that is also a path. Execution starts at $ and walks the grid, turning on the slashes; the = runs are cells being counted up.
EXPERT_ID.fact: SNUSP takes Brainfuck’s tape and makes it two-dimensional: the instruction pointer travels a path through the source, turning on / and \, entering and leaving subroutines as the path crosses itself. $ marks the start.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Excerpt — the alphabet looks familiar, but watch the output commands: the dots fall in strict groups of eight, because every character leaves the machine as eight single-bit cells.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Brainbool is Brainfuck rebuilt on boolean memory: every cell holds a single bit, input arrives bit by bit and output leaves bit by bit, so printing one character takes eight output commands. Same alphabet, crueller machine.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Excerpt — only five distinct characters exist in this language: > < * [ ]. There is no separate output command hiding anywhere; * is doing double duty.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Smallfuck strips Brainfuck to five commands — > < * [ ] — on a tape of single-bit cells: * flips the current bit, and a cell is output by flipping it as the pointer leaves it inside a loop. The original spec even gives the tape a finite length.

EXPERT_ID.note: // A complete program, and the slashes are the whole syntax: /pattern/replacement/ rewrites the text that follows, over and over, and whatever survives is the output.
EXPERT_ID.fact: /// — pronounced “slashes” — has exactly one construct: /pattern/replacement/, applied repeatedly to the rest of the text. With no pattern left to match, the remaining text is printed. It is Turing complete, which surprises everyone the first time.

EXPERT_ID.note: // A complete program, six characters of machinery around the text: parentheses push a string onto the stack, and S prints the top of it.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Underload (by ais523) is a stack machine whose stack holds strings: ( … ) pushes, S prints, ~ swaps, : duplicates, * joins two strings and ^ executes the top one as code. (Hello, World!)S really is the whole Hello World.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Excerpt — the entire language is on show: one combinator, i, and one symbol, *, meaning “apply”. There is nothing else to learn, and that is the problem.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Iota (Chris Barker) has a single combinator, ι = λx.((x S) K), written i, with * for function application. Every program — including this Hello World — is just i’s and *’s in prefix order, yet it can express any lambda term.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Excerpt — the whole program is a binary string. Each 0 and 1 extends a combinator expression; there are no other characters in the language.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Jot (Chris Barker) is combinatory logic written in binary: a program is any string of 0s and 1s, where 1 applies the accumulated function and 0 wraps it in S and K combinators. Every binary string is a valid program.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Excerpt — backtick means “apply”, and s, k and i are the only functions that exist. The characters of the greeting are encoded in the shape of the expression itself.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Lazy K is the untyped lambda calculus reduced to the S, K and I combinators with ` for application — no variables, no literals. Input and output are Church-encoded lists of numbers, so even “Hello” has to be built out of pure functions.

EXPERT_ID.note: // An ordered list of fractions and a starting integer: that is a complete program in this language. Nothing else exists — no instructions, no variables, no output statement.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Fractran (John Conway) runs by multiplying a single integer by the first fraction in the list that yields another integer, and repeating. Prime factorisation does all the bookkeeping — its famous PRIMEGAME list generates the prime numbers.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Excerpt — backtick applies one function to the next and .x prints the character x. There are no variables and no keywords anywhere in the language.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Unlambda (David Madore) is functional programming stripped to combinators — `k, `s and `i — plus .x, which prints x. It was designed to make functional programming feel as awkward as Brainfuck makes imperative programming feel.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Excerpt — after each instruction the code encrypts itself, so the same character never means the same thing twice. This is the deep pool; it belongs here.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Malbolge (Ben Olmstead, 1998) encrypts its own code after every instruction. Nobody wrote a working program in it for two years — the first Hello World was found by a search algorithm, not a human.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Excerpt — only six characters ever appear in this language: [ ] ( ) ! +. Underneath the noise this is a language you have almost certainly used.
EXPERT_ID.fact: JSFuck writes any JavaScript using only []()!+ : brackets and coercion between booleans, strings and numbers spell out letters. It runs in any browser console.

EXPERT_ID.note: // Raw excerpt, exactly as stored — no visible symbols substituted. In Expert you read the real file: spaces, tabs and linefeeds, and nothing else carries meaning.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Whitespace (Edwin Brady & Chris Morris, released 1 April 2003) uses only spaces, tabs and linefeeds — every other character is ignored as a comment, so a program can hide invisibly inside ordinary text.

EXPERT_ID.code:
DO ,1 <- #13
PLEASE DO ,1 SUB #1 <- #238
DO ,1 SUB #2 <- #108
PLEASE READ OUT ,1
PLEASE GIVE UP
EXPERT_ID.note: // The manners are load-bearing: PLEASE too rarely and the compiler refuses you for rudeness; too often and it rejects you for grovelling.
EXPERT_ID.fact: INTERCAL (1972), by Don Woods and Jim Lyon, is the original parody language — and the ancestor of half this pool. The compiler counts your PLEASEs and rejects programs that are too rude or too polite.

EXPERT_ID.note: // The string is pushed backwards, then printed character by character as the pointer loops the grid. An old friend — but in Expert it is the easiest thing on the menu.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Befunge-93 (Chris Pressey, 1993) runs on a 2D grid: > < ^ v steer the instruction pointer, and the program can rewrite its own grid as it runs — designed, on purpose, to be as hard as possible to compile.

EXPERT_ID.note: // A source file that is also a floor plan: walls and openings steer execution through the maze, and instructions are picked up on the way through.
EXPERT_ID.fact: Labyrinth (Martin Ender) is a 2D language whose source is a maze — the cells around the instruction pointer decide its direction of travel, and characters like ( ) and " are instructions collected on the way through.

EXPERT_TWO.fact: Thue (John Colagioia, 2000): a program is a set of ::= substitution rules, ~ marks output, and execution rewrites the starting string until no rule applies.

EXPERT_TWO.note: // Two-stage round — stage 1 of 2: pick the family. Get it wrong and the round ends immediately. Get it right and you pick the exact language, for the same +100 / −50 stakes.
EXPERT_TWO.fact: /// (“slashes”) has one construct — /pattern/replacement/ applied to the following text until nothing matches; what survives is printed. Turing complete, somehow.

EXPERT_TWO.note: // Two-stage round — stage 1 of 2: pick the family. Get it wrong and the round ends immediately. Get it right and you pick the exact language, for the same +100 / −50 stakes.
EXPERT_TWO.fact: Iota (Chris Barker) builds everything from one combinator, ι = λx.((x S) K), written i, with * for application. This fragment is nothing but i’s and *’s — there is nothing else in the language.

EXPERT_TWO.note: // Two-stage round — stage 1 of 2: pick the family. Get it wrong and the round ends immediately. Get it right and you pick the exact language, for the same +100 / −50 stakes.
EXPERT_TWO.fact: Lazy K reduces the lambda calculus to the S, K and I combinators with ` for application; input and output are Church-encoded lists, so the greeting is encoded in the expression’s shape.

EXPERT_TWO.note: // Two-stage round — stage 1 of 2: pick the family. Get it wrong and the round ends immediately. Get it right and you pick the exact language, for the same +100 / −50 stakes.
EXPERT_TWO.fact: SNUSP makes Brainfuck two-dimensional: execution walks a path through the source starting at $, turning on / and \, with the tape waiting at the end of the path.

EXPERT_TWO.note: // Two-stage round — stage 1 of 2: pick the family. Get it wrong and the round ends immediately. Get it right and you pick the exact language, for the same +100 / −50 stakes. Watch the output commands: they fall in groups of eight.
EXPERT_TWO.fact: Brainbool is Brainfuck on boolean memory — every cell is one bit, so each character is printed as eight separate output operations.

EXPERT_TWO.note: // Two-stage round — stage 1 of 2: pick the family. Get it wrong and the round ends immediately. Get it right and you pick the exact language, for the same +100 / −50 stakes. Count the distinct characters: there are five.
EXPERT_TWO.fact: Smallfuck keeps only > < * [ ] from Brainfuck, on a bit tape: * flips the current cell, and output happens as a side effect of the flip-and-move idiom.

EXPERT_TWO.note: // Two-stage round — stage 1 of 2: pick the family. Get it wrong and the round ends immediately. Get it right and you pick the exact language, for the same +100 / −50 stakes.
EXPERT_TWO.fact: FALSE (Wouter van Oortmerssen, 1993) is a postfix stack language of single-character symbols; the string literal pushes, and ß flushes the output.

EXPERT_TWO.note: // Two-stage round — stage 1 of 2: pick the family. Get it wrong and the round ends immediately. Get it right and you pick the exact language, for the same +100 / −50 stakes.
EXPERT_TWO.fact: Underload keeps a stack of strings: ( … ) pushes, S prints, ~ swaps, : duplicates, * concatenates and ^ executes the top string as code.

EXPERT_TWO.note: // Two-stage round — stage 1 of 2: pick the family. Get it wrong and the round ends immediately. Get it right and you pick the exact language, for the same +100 / −50 stakes.
EXPERT_TWO.fact: Fractran (John Conway): multiply one integer by the first listed fraction that keeps it whole, repeat. Prime factorisation is the memory.

EXPERT_PAIR.fact: Both excerpts are Brainfuck — different Hello World constructions (one builds its cells with a ×10 loop, the other with nested loops), but the same eight commands: > < + - . , [ ].

EXPERT_PAIR.fact: Both are Ook! — the same one word with its three endings, . ? and !, paired into Brainfuck’s eight commands. Different stretches of the program, identical alphabet.

EXPERT_PAIR.note: // Pairing round — two different excerpts. Are they the same language? Different programs, possibly the same tongue.
EXPERT_PAIR.fact: Both are Thue: ::= rules on the left, ~ marking output. The second program simply splits the greeting across two rules — same rewriting machine.

EXPERT_PAIR.fact: Not the same. The first is Unlambda — the .x commands print characters directly. The second is Lazy K, pure S/K/I combinators with no printing primitive at all: its output is encoded, not spelled out.

EXPERT_PAIR.note: // Pairing round — two different excerpts, both by the same designer, both combinator calculus. Are they the same language?
EXPERT_PAIR.fact: Not the same — siblings, not twins. Iota writes its single combinator as i with * for application; Jot (same designer, Chris Barker) encodes combinatory logic as a pure binary string of 0s and 1s.

EXPERT_PAIR.note: // Pairing round — two different excerpts, both tape machines with brackets. Are they the same language?
EXPERT_PAIR.fact: Not the same. Brainfuck has eight commands — note the + and . everywhere. Smallfuck kept only > < * [ ] and replaced increment-and-print with a single bit-flip, *.

EXPERT_PAIR.note: // Pairing round — two different excerpts, both string-rewriting languages. Are they the same language?
EXPERT_PAIR.fact: Not the same. Thue separates its rules with ::= and marks output with ~, with the rule list closed off before the data. /// has no rule list at all — each /pattern/replacement/ sits inline in the text it rewrites.
